As mentioned in the section, the cost to operate these technologies to respond to dynamic pricing might incur additional costs (e.g., subscription service), which is not accounted for in our modeling. If a customer already has the technology installed, we only compute operation and maintenance costs. This is determined by the existing saturation of each control technology. Further, we consider the annual bill savings to characterize the benefits. There might be other benefits (e.g., aesthetics of a thermostat) which are not included in the benefits characterization. Finally, since we evaluate the end-use response at the cluster level, each customer’s benefit aka bill savings within the cluster will be the same for each end use. In reality, there would be considerable variations, but these variations are not accounted for in this study. Technology payback period The final metric developed to characterize the economics of responding to dynamic pricing is the technology payback period. Payback period refers to the period in years that is required to recover the upfront costs of a DR control technology in the form of bill savings. In addition to the cost benefit ratio, it is a useful metric to analyze because customers might not be willing to install a certain technology to enable response if they are unable to recover the costs in a short period of time. Prior studies have shown that technology adoption reduces steeply for payback periods longer than 5 years (Wilson et al. 2017). Hence, if the bill savings are not substantial in comparison to the costs, then, even a technology that appears cost-effective from an annualized 23 cost perspective might not experience huge uptake. In this study, we compute the payback period as the shown in the equation below: 𝑃𝐵𝑃 = (𝐼𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙 𝑐𝑜𝑠𝑡)/(𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑙 𝑠𝑎𝑣𝑖𝑛𝑔𝑠 − 𝑂&𝑀 𝑐𝑜𝑠𝑡𝑠 − 𝑓𝑖𝑛𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑐𝑜𝑠𝑡𝑠) Where initial cost is the total upfront cost of the technology. Bill savings reflects annual stream of benefits, and O&M costs and financing costs reflect annual cost streams. 3 Results 3.1 Price profiles Figure 10 shows the distribution of hourly prices for each utility, each price scenario (year, forecast scenario, and tariff design scenario), and for two customer classes: residential (top) and Large C&I (bottom). Hourly dynamic prices for the 2019 Full tariff scenario were developed for previous work. For residential customers, these prices had median values of $0.24/kWh for PG&E, $0.21/kWh for SCE, and $0.32/kWh for SDG&E. For all utilities, the maximum hourly price was 4.5-5x the median price, and prices were zero in some hours. In the 2019 Medium scenario, median prices rise approximately 3 cents/kWh for all utilities, while maximum values decrease 15-25 cents/kWh and minimums increase to $0.13/kWh. In the 2019 Mild scenario, prices continue to concentrate at slightly higher values; median prices are 0.30, 0.27, and 0.39 $/kWh for PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E, respectively, while maximum values are approximately 2x median.
